answer.recommendation: Aim for roughly 10 to 12 hard weekly sets per muscle, since 10 or more weekly sets beat fewer than 5 in a high-grade meta-analysis [1] and a 12-week trial in trained adults found 12 sets worked as well as 24 [2]. Go higher only if recovery allows, because a 12-week trial in trained adults found 24 weekly sets gave no more growth than 12 [3].
answer.why: The strongest evidence is a meta-analysis of 15 trials showing 10 or more weekly sets produced larger gains than fewer than 5, with 0.37% more muscle size per additional weekly set [1]. A trial in resistance-trained men found 30 weekly sets raised quadriceps thickness 6.8% versus 2.1% with 6 sets [4]. A preprint suggests diminishing returns, with the marginal gain per set roughly halving between 10 and 20 sets, but it is not peer reviewed and cannot carry the advice [5]. The most similar population, 40 trained adults including 18 women, showed no extra growth from 24 sets versus 12 (5.6% vs 5.1%, p=0.61), with worse recovery scores at 24 sets [2]. That trial is small, so it does not prove a plateau, and none of the evidence matches an intermediate woman closely, so confidence is low [3].

positions.best_counterargument: A high-grade meta-analysis found a graded dose-response in which 10 or more weekly sets beat fewer than 5. A trial in resistance-trained men found 30 weekly sets gave 6.8% quadriceps growth against 2.1% with 6 sets. A single 12-week trial in 40 trained adults is a thin basis for declaring a plateau.

answer.what_would_change_this: Larger trials in trained women comparing 12 sets with higher volumes would settle this [3]. If they showed continued gains above 12 weekly sets, I would raise the target [3]. A plateau at or below 12 sets would support staying there [3].
answer.applies_to_you: You are a trained woman with 3 years of training, so you sit between the untrained women in one trial [7] and the trained men in another [4]. The meta-analysis was mostly young men who were untrained or recreationally trained [1]. The trial closest to you included 18 women with at least 2 years of training [2]. Training 4 days per week gives room to spread sets, and frequency does not matter much once weekly volume is equated (p=0.42) [6].
answer.practical_protocol: Next week, do about 10 to 12 hard sets per muscle, spread over your 4 days [1] [2]. Weekly volume is what matters, not how it is split across sessions (p=0.42) [6]. If recovery is good after a few weeks, add sets gradually, expecting smaller returns for each one [5]. If recovery worsens, return to 12 sets, since 24 sets came with worse recovery scores [2].
